defects.claim: GitGraph export rewrites " to ' in branch names, so distinct branches collide and reimport rejects a duplicate branch
Block parser accepts a dangling trailing link operator (`A B -->`) and creates an A → B edge instead of a syntax error
Flowchart style grouping spreads the existing ID array for each node, making it quadratic in a shared style group's size
Class and ER writers silently drop a box's header rows, losing the class/entity name
defects.scenario: a node with `rows: [{ kind: 'header', text: 'Order' }, { kind: 'label', text: 'id: int' }]` written as a class diagram: `classParts` only collects `label` and `field` rows, so the header text is never read. The class name falls back to `node.id`, or to the first label row (`id: int` becomes the name). No warning is raised. `er/write.ts:23` (`entityParts`) filters to `label`/`field` the same way, so an entity's header name is lost too. It should take a header row as the name (or at least warn that it was dropped).
defects.cause: row-kind switch misses `header`

defects.claim: Flowchart node metadata keys other than shape and label are dropped without a warning
defects.scenario: `A@{ shape: rect, icon: "fa:user", w: 80, img: "x.png" }` reads only `shape` and `label`. `icon`, `img`, `w`, `h`, `pos`, `constraint` and so on vanish, and the import's warnings never mention them. Every other unsupported input in these readers is reported through `warnings.list(...)`.
defects.cause: option silently dropped on one path

defects.claim: Lexer reads A--oB / A--xB as an open line to node oB instead of a circle/cross edge to B
defects.scenario: the tail `[ox](?![\p{L}\p{N}_])` refuses a head that is followed by a letter. `A--oB` therefore lexes as link `--` (no head, and not opening a label, because the next char is not whitespace) followed by the word `oB`. The result is edge A→oB with `markerEnd: null`. Mermaid's lexer (`\-\-+[-xo>]`) takes `--o` greedily, which gives A→B with a circle end. Mermaid's own docs warn about exactly this reading for ids that start with o/x. The import silently produces a different graph (a node `oB` instead of `B`, and the wrong end).
defects.cause: lookahead diverges from Mermaid's link token

defects.claim: Block writer moves a group holding no blocks to the end of its row, shifting the grid on round-trip
defects.scenario:
`block-beta
 columns 3
 a
 block:g
 end
 b` reads into nodes a, b and an empty container g. On write, `first({cluster: g})` is `Infinity` (no nodes), so `level` sorts g after b and emits `a`, `b`, `block:g end`. g moves from grid cell 2 to cell 3, and b from 3 to 2. The reader kept g's position in its parent's `members` order, which the writer ignores. Top level has no members list at all, so the order is guessed from node order.
defects.cause: item order derived from first node index; empty clusters have none

defects.claim: Architecture writer silently falls back to R/L for non-compass routedPorts
defects.scenario: an edge with no `fromPort`/`toPort` but `routedPorts: { from: 'ne', to: 'sw' }`: the warning check only looks at `e.fromPort`/`e.toPort`, but `end()` is passed `e.routedPorts?.from`. `PORT_SIDES.get('ne')` misses, so the edge is written `:R`/`L:` with no warning that the routed sides were changed.
defects.cause: warning checks a different port source than the write

defects.claim: gitGraph writer spells a main branch name containing " differently in front matter and in branch statements, so the file fails to read back
defects.scenario: `mainBranch: 'a"b'`: the front matter writes `mainBranchName: "a\"b"` (JSON, which keeps the quote). Every command naming that branch goes through `branchName` → `quoted`, which turns `"` into `'`, giving `checkout "a'b"` / `merge "a'b"`. On read the main branch is `a"b`, and `checkout a'b` names a branch never made, so `replayGitGraph` errors and `readMermaidGitGraph` throws.
defects.cause: one name encoded two ways in one file

defects.claim: Gantt writer leaves ';' unescaped in names, titles and sections, and '#'/';' raw in task ids, so Mermaid's gantt lexer cuts the token short
defects.scenario: a gantt task named `Build; test`, or a section or title holding `;`, is written as-is (spelledLine spells only `#` and `:`). A task id `a#1` or `a;b` passes `plain` (it checks only whitespace, commas and tag words) and is written raw after the colon. Mermaid's gantt grammar reads task data as `":"[^#\n;]+` and titles and sections up to `#`/`;`, so real Mermaid truncates or rejects these lines. The package's own reader doesn't treat `;` as syntax, so a round-trip test passes while the file breaks in Mermaid. The journey writer handles the same characters (it strips `#` and `;`), so the two kinds disagree.
defects.cause: spelled set missing `;`; id check missing `#` and `;`

defects.claim: Flowchart lexer splits A--text-->B (link text with no space after --) into three nodes instead of one labeled link
defects.scenario: `opens` is true only when the `--`/`==`/`-.` is followed by whitespace. For `A--text-->B`, the lexer emits `--` as a link with no end, then the word `text`, then `-->`. The parser builds the chain A --- text --> B: a phantom node `text` and two edges. Mermaid's START_LINK rule (`\s*[xo<]?\-\-\s*`) allows no whitespace there, so Mermaid reads one edge A→B labeled "text".
defects.cause: link text opens only when whitespace follows

defects.claim: Flowchart reader drops every plain mention of a node whose id is also some link's id
defects.scenario: `flowchart TD\n  A e1@--> B\n  e1 --> C`. `edgeIdsOf` collects `e1`, and `mention` returns early for any ref `e1` that has no shape. It does that whether or not the ref carries `@{…}` metadata. So node `e1` is never created, and a spurious "edge metadata was dropped" warning is raised. `link()` still pushes an edge `e1 → C` to a node that does not exist. The early return should apply only to a ref that carries metadata (`ref.meta !== undefined`) and is not otherwise a node.
defects.cause: edge-id test ignores whether the ref has metadata

defects.claim: Flowchart lexer cannot read a circle- or cross-ended link that has text between its dashes
defects.scenario: `A o-- text --o B` (or `x-- text --x`). The LINK match gives lead `o`, body `--` and no tail. The guard `(lead === 'o' || lead === 'x') && tail !== lead` returns false before the text-link path (`opens`/`linkText`) is tried. `o` is then lexed as a word, and the parser throws "expected the end of the statement, found "o"". The same link with `|text|` reads, so a valid Mermaid link form is refused. For an opening link, the guard should compare the lead with the closer's head that `linkText` returns.
defects.cause: lead/tail check runs before the text-link closer is known

defects.claim: C4 relationship technology given with an empty label comes back as the label after a round-trip
defects.scenario: `Rel(a, b, "", "HTTPS")`. The reader builds the label from `[text(label), "[tech]"]` and gets `[HTTPS]`. On write, `/^(.*?)(?: \[([^\]]*)\])?$/` needs a space before `[`, so `m[1]` is `[HTTPS]` and `m[2]` is undefined. The output is `Rel(a, b, "[HTTPS]")`, which moves the technology into the description/label argument. The element path (`elementParts`) keeps the two apart, but the relationship path does not. The writer regex should also take a label that is only `[tech]`.
defects.cause: label/technology split regex requires a leading space

defects.claim: A gitGraph directive that sets only the main branch is still warned as dropped when the branch name holds an apostrophe
defects.scenario: `%%{init: {"gitGraph": {"mainBranchName": "O'Brien"}}}%%`. `BRANCH_NAME` reads the name correctly. `directiveJson` then replaces every `'` with `"`, the JSON fails to parse, and `onlyMainBranch(null)` is false. `directives` is not decremented, so `readPageName` warns that the configuration directives were dropped, although the only thing they set was read.
defects.cause: blanket quote replacement corrupts values that contain apostrophes

defects.claim: Block reader accepts `columns 0` and `block:id:0` without a warning, and the writer then drops them
defects.scenario: `block-beta\n columns 0\n a b`. The parser reads n=0 and `walk` sets `top = 0`, which the grid layout then clamps to 1 with no warning. Writing that page back, `gridCount` drops the 0 and warns "whole numbers from 1". So the reader and writer disagree about whether 0 is a valid count, and the read gives no warning for a value the page does not honor.
defects.cause: no validation of counts on read

defects.claim: Flowchart writer silently writes a path outline node as a rectangle, with no warning
defects.scenario: a node whose `outline` is a `Path` (the `Outline` type is `BuiltinOutline | string | Path`) is written. `brackets` is undefined, but the warning only fires when `typeof outline === 'string'`, so the node comes out as `id["…"]` (a rectangle) with no warning. It should warn as it does for an unknown string outline. The block writer (`block/write.ts` `block()`) warns whenever `brackets === undefined`, so the two writers handle the same case differently.
defects.cause: warning gated on a string outline

defects.claim: Architecture and C4 writers drop the page direction without a warning
defects.scenario: a graph page with `direction: 'down'` (or `'up'`/`'left'`) and notation `architecture` is written. Mermaid architecture has no direction statement, and `readArchitecture` always reads `direction: 'right'`, so the round trip turns the page sideways and `warnings` says nothing about it. `writeC4` likewise never reads `page.direction`. Every other dropped property in these writers (positions, styles, labels, ports) gets a warning.
defects.cause: missing drop warning

defects.claim: Block parser reads a line with two link operators in a row followed by two blocks as a chain instead of rejecting it
defects.scenario: `a --> --> b c` (or `a b --> --> c`) collects items `[a, b, c]` and two links. The check only compares counts (`ends.length === links.length + 1` and `ends.length === items.length`), not that blocks and links alternate, so it passes and reads as `a → b → c` instead of throwing "cannot read … as blocks joined by links". The order in which items and links appeared is never recorded.
defects.cause: count check instead of alternation check

defects.claim: Flowchart, block and architecture writers rename ids their own readers accept (node-1, 1, a.b)
defects.scenario: The flowchart lexer's and block parser's `WORD` (`[\p{L}\p{N}_](?:[\p{L}\p{N}_]|[-.](?=…))*`) and architecture's `ID` (`[\p{L}\p{N}_][\p{L}\p{N}_-]*`) read `node-1`, `1` and `a.b` as ids. All three writers call `mermaidIds(…, { unicode: true })`, which only keeps ids matching `^[\p{L}_][\p{L}\p{N}_]*$`. So reading `flowchart TD\n 1 --> node-1` and writing it back gives `n1 --> node_1`: every id with a hyphen, a dot or a leading digit is renamed on a plain round trip. In the block writer, the reader's own minted anonymous group id `block-1` can never be written as itself either: once a span or an edge forces it to be named, it comes back as `block_1`. The writers should pass an `id` regex matching what their reader takes, as the class and ER writers already do.
defects.cause: writer's id grammar narrower than reader's

defects.claim: mermaidIds treats flowchart keywords case-insensitively, so End, Graph and Style nodes are needlessly renamed
defects.scenario: `words` lowercases every keyword, and `valid` tests `words.has(id.toLowerCase())`. A node whose id is `End` or `END` (Mermaid's own documented fix for the `end` trap) or `Style` is judged reserved and written as `End_`. The flowchart reader's keyword checks are case-sensitive (`word(t, 'end')` in parse.ts, and `REST_KEYWORDS.has(word[0])` in lex.ts), so `End` would read back unchanged. Result: a flowchart with `Start --> End` comes back as `Start --> End_`, with the node's id changed.
defects.cause: case-folded keyword set vs case-sensitive reader

defects.claim: C4 reader accepts BiRel_U, BiRel_Back and RelIndex_Back, which the writer cannot produce, and reads BiRel_Back as one-way
defects.scenario: `REL` allows any of `Rel|BiRel|RelIndex` with any suffix. `BiRel_U(a, b)` reads with ports n/s, but the writer says "Mermaid C4 has no direction for a two-way or backward relationship" and drops them. So the reader and writer answer differently whether a two-way relationship has a direction. `BiRel_Back(a, b)` takes `back` and sets `markerEnd: null`, so a relationship named bidirectional reads as a one-headed backward arrow.
defects.cause: reader grammar wider than the macros Mermaid and the writer have

defects.claim: Class writer keeps extra name lines as members in one case and silently drops them in the other
defects.scenario: rows `[label A, label B, divider, label x, divider, label m()]` give `names = [A, B]`. With two dividers (`rest.length > 1`), attributes are `rest[0]` and `B` vanishes without a warning. With zero or one divider, `names.slice(1)` is kept as members. The same second line is kept on one path and dropped on the other.
defects.cause: names.slice(1) left out of the divided branch

defects.claim: A class name or label written as <<…>> reads back as an annotation, losing the name
defects.scenario: the reader yields name row `<<x>>` for `class A["<<x>>"]`, or a user names a box `<<Service>>` with no annotations. classParts treats every `<<…>>` line above the first divider as an annotation, so the class is written as `class A { <<x>> }`. The label is gone and an annotation has been added. The writer never spells the brackets to stop this.
defects.cause: annotation detected by text shape alone

defects.claim: Block writer turns any dash pattern into Mermaid's dotted link without a warning
defects.scenario: an edge with `colors.dash: [10, 2]` is written as `-.-`, which reads back as `[4, 4]`. The function warns about stroke, label and width but never about dash, whereas the flowchart writer keeps a non-dotted dash through `linkStyle` and other kinds call `dropEdgeColors`. The pattern changes silently.
defects.cause: dash missing from dropped-style warnings

defects.claim: Class diagram note text loses an `&` that comes right before a backslash
defects.scenario: a `note` shape whose text is `R&\D`. `spelled()` runs `spelledBreaks` first, and it leaves the `&` alone because nothing after it looks like an entity yet. Only after that does `.replace(/\\/g, '#92;')` turn the backslash into `#92;`, so the line written is `note "R\D"`. On read, `decodeEntities(l, true)` matches `\` as one HTML numeric reference, and the note comes back as `R\D`. The `&` is silently lost. It should come back as `R&\D`: the `&` needs to be spelled `#38;` once the `#92;` exists, which means escaping `\` before `spelledBreaks` runs.
defects.cause: an entity is added after the `&` guard has already run

defects.claim: Class and ER writers drop a connector's dash pattern without a warning
defects.scenario: an edge with `colors.dash = [2, 6]`. All three writers write any dash as a dotted line (`..`, `..`, `-.-`), and each reader reads that back as `[4, 4]`. The class and ER writers list `dash` as kept in `dropEdgeColors`, so nothing warns. The block writer warns about stroke, label and width, but not dash. The pattern changes with no warning. The flowchart writer handles the same case properly, writing the custom pattern as a `linkStyle … stroke-dasharray`, so the kinds answer one question two ways. Expected: a warning whenever the dash is not `[4, 4]` (or not `DOTTED_DASH`).
defects.cause: "has a dash" is checked, not which dash

defects.claim: Flowchart writer writes an explicit solid dash (`dash: []`) as a dotted/dashed Mermaid line
defects.scenario: a graph page whose edge has `colors: { dash: [] }` (solid, as `paint.ts` and the DOT and draw-XML writers read an empty dash; Mermaid's own `dashOf` also yields `[]` for `stroke-dasharray:` with no value) is written with `dash !== undefined` as the test, so the flowchart writes `-.-`/`-.->`, the block diagram `-.-`, the class diagram `..`, and the ER diagram `..`. Read back, those edges carry `dash: [4, 4]`, so a solid connector turns dotted. It should be written as a solid line, the way the DOT writer's `dash.length > 0` test treats it.
defects.cause: the Mermaid writers and the other writers decide "dashed" differently (`!== undefined` against `length > 0`)

defects.claim: Journey writer checks a title or section name for emptiness before stripping its syntax characters, so a name that is empty after stripping is still written
defects.scenario: `data.title` is `"#;"` or a section is named `":"`. The guard (`data.title?.trim()`, `section.name.trim() !== ''`) tests the raw text, then `plain` strips every character, so the writer emits a bare `  title ` or `  section ` line. Mermaid's journey grammar needs text after `title`/`section`, so the file fails to parse there. The local reader accepts it, which hides the problem. Step names avoid this because `stepName` runs after `plain` and falls back to `(untitled)`. The emptiness test should run on the stripped text, as it does for steps and actors.
defects.cause: emptiness checked before `plain`, not after

defects.claim: Gantt writer emits a bare `section` or `title` line for an empty name
defects.scenario: a gantt whose section `name` is `''` (the local reader produces this from a bare `section` line), or whose `title` is `''` or only whitespace. The writer tests only `!== undefined`, so it writes `  section ` / `  title `. Mermaid's gantt grammar needs text after either keyword, so its parser rejects the file. An empty name should be treated as no name: the section's tasks join the one before, with the existing warning, and the title line is left out.
defects.cause: `!== undefined` used where an empty-text test is needed

defects.claim: Block writer wrongly warns that a grid skip of 0 was dropped
defects.scenario: a grid layout whose `skips` gives an item `0` (no gap). `gridCount` rounds it to 0, finds `whole < 1`, and warns "Mermaid block spaces are whole numbers from 1; others were dropped." The output is right (no `space` line), but the warning reports a loss that did not happen. A skip of 0 should be read as no skip, with no warning.
defects.cause: gridCount's lower bound of 1 is applied to skips, where 0 is valid

defects.claim: Block writer omits the id of a container whose id looks like an auto-generated `block-N`, so it reads back under a different id
defects.scenario: the writer leaves the id off any container matching `/^block-\d+$/` that has no span, edge or style. The reader then gives each unnamed `block … end` the next free `block-N`, counting in the order the groups appear in the file (`IdMint.next('block')`). That is not always the original id:
defects.cause: assumes every `block-N` id would be minted again as itself
